title: TB6-07307
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the "principal Appellant") and XXXX XXXX (the "female Appellant") are citizens of China. They appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection. They have not submitted new evidence in support of their appeal. They ask that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection or, in the alternative, refer their claims back to the RPD for redetermination.
Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal. Background

The Appellants alleged before the RPD that they were suffering from ailments in China that medical intervention could not resolve. They were introduced to the practice of Falun Gong by a friend and began practicing Falun Gong in February 2015. They allege they came to Canada for tourism on XXXX XXXX, 2015. While in Canada, they learned that the PSB had raided their underground Falun Gong group and had arrested three of their fellow practitioners. They also learned that the PSB were seeking to arrest them and had attended their home in search of them.

The Appellant's application for refugee protection was heard over two sittings on March 10 and March 24, 2016. In a decision of May 17, 2016, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claims finding that the Appellants were not credible.
The Appellants submit that the RPD's credibility findings were flawed and erred in its treatment of their documentary evidence.

The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal.

The RAD concludes from its statutory analysis that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD's decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the Appellant, the RPD erred. ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL Credibility Female Appellant's Medical Evidence

The female Appellant alleged that the reason she was prompted to take up the illegal practice of Falun Gong in China was due to the problems she was experiencing with menstruation. The RAD found that the female Appellant's testimony was internally inconsistent and inconsistent with her Basis of Claim (BoC) narrative as well as the medical documents she tendered as corroboration. The RPD also found that the female Appellant's testimony evolved when confronted with those inconsistencies and that her testimony about when her health problems started, when she started seeing the doctor for this problem, and when she started medication for the problem varied substantially during the hearing. The RAD notes that the inconsistency between the female Appellant's testimony and the medical booklet not only undermines the Appellant's testimony but also undermines the genuineness of the medical booklet itself. The RPD also found that the medical booklet tendered by the Appellant was further undermined by the fact that falsified documents are prevalent in China.2

The RPD went on to find that, on a balance of probabilities, the female Appellant did not have the medical problems that she alleged and that she tendered a fraudulent medical booklet to advance a fraudulent refugee claim.

The Appellants do not dispute that the female Appellants' testimony was inconsistent or that her testimony evolved. Nor do they dispute the RPD's findings with regard to the medical booklet. They do in essence argue that the numerous inconsistencies in her testimony can be explained by the fact that she was pregnant at the time and was experiencing symptoms of fatigue as well as memory and concentration problems among others. They argue that the letter they tendered at the commencement of the second sitting indicated that she was experiencing these symptoms and the RPD erred by giving the medical letter little weight. They argue that it was unreasonable for the RPD to dismiss the letter on the basis that she failed to advise the panel that she was suffering from these symptoms at the time of the hearing.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument in this regard. Prior to the resumption of the second hearing, Counsel for the Appellants tendered the letter with the argument that the female Appellant had memory and concentration difficulties spanning back to the time of the first hearing. However, the RAD notes that the letter indicates that the Appellant was seen eleven days after the first sitting. The RAD also notes that the letter does state that the Appellant was suffering from those symptoms at the time of the hearing. As noted by the RPD, the female Appellant did not profess to having concentration or memory problems at the time of the first hearing. Furthermore, the RAD notes that the symptoms were subjectively identified in that those symptoms are based on the self-report of the female Appellant. There is no indication that the doctor administered any objective tests or physical examination to verify the female Appellant's self-report.

After its own review of the evidence, the RAD agrees with the RPD and finds that the medical note does not excuse the multiplicity of significant inconsistencies and contradictions made in the female Appellant's testimony. The RAD agrees with the RPD and finds that the female Appellant was not suffering from a serious medical condition in China as alleged. The RAD notes that the sole reason the female Appellant alleges she engaged in the illegal practice of Falun Gong was to mitigate her medical condition. Having found that she was not suffering from that medical condition, the RAD finds that the female Appellant's allegation that she engaged in the practice of Falun Gong is significantly undermined.

The RAD further agrees with the RPD that, on a balance of probabilities, the female Appellant's allegation that she was a Falun Gong practitioner in China was made to advance a fraudulent refugee claim. The RAD finds that, given the Appellants have alleged that they practiced Falun Gong in China together and joined an underground practice group together, the finding that the female Appellant has advanced a fraudulent refugee claim significantly undermines the principal Appellant's claim that he was a Falun Gong practitioner in China. Principal Appellant's Medical Evidence

The principal Appellant also alleged that he was prompted to engage in the illegal practice of Falun Gong because of a medical condition that both Western and traditional Chinese medicine could not resolve. He alleges that he suffers from nervous headaches which first began in 2012 and that he received hospital treatments. The Appellants tendered a medical booklet which details the principal Appellant's medical condition. The RPD gave little weight to the booklet. The RPD noted that the booklet was dated in 2014 and purports to summarize the principal Appellant's medical history regarding his diagnosis and treatment for nervous headaches two years prior. The RPD noted that the Appellants failed to tender detailed medical information and reports of the principal Appellant's alleged medical condition and treatment from 2012 to 2014. The RPD found that the absence of detailed medical records for the entire period of his alleged illness and treatment and the prevalence of fraudulent documents in China undermined the weight that could be given to the booklet.

The Appellants submit that there is nothing in the medical booklet that suggests any impropriety or that the information contained in it was not accurate. They further argue that it was improper for the RPD to rely on the prevalence of fraudulent documents in China to undermine the credibility of the principal Appellant's medical booklet.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument in this regard. The RAD notes that the documentary evidence in the record reveals that it is difficult to verify the reliability of the medical booklets because they are easy to obtain from hospitals and they are handwritten.3 More importantly, the RAD notes that the medical booklets of both Appellants are issued by the same source, the Tianjin Hospital. The RAD also notes that, although both Appellants alleged that their medical conditions and treatment extended over many years, neither of them tendered full medical records of their entire treatment for their alleged illnesses. Having found that the Appellants tendered a fraudulent medical booklet as corroboration of the female Appellant's medical condition, the RAD finds no weight can be given to the medical booklet of the principal Appellant. The RAD finds the principal Appellant's explanation that he lost his previous medical records to be a convenient explanation for the absence of medical records that he ought to be able to tender.

The RAD finds that the absence of detailed medical evidence of the alleged illness and treatment, in the context of having tendered a fraudulent medical document and having found that the female Appellant was not treated for a medical condition as they alleged, the RAD finds that the Appellants' allegation that the principal Appellant suffered from a medical condition and that was the reason he began the practice of Falun Gong is not credible. PSB Visits to the Appellant's Home

The Appellant have alleged that they had traveled to Canada in XXXX XXXX 2015 on their own passports, using valid visitor's visas. The Appellant alleged that the PSB first attended their home on XXXX XXXX, 2015 after they arrived in Canada and that they made two visits to their home seeking information about them since then.

The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the Appellants' allegations that the PSB made multiple visits to their home. The RPD found the alleged PSB's behaviour in attending the Appellants' residence three times and demanding information about their whereabouts is inconsistent with the documentary evidence that describes the ability of the PSB to monitor its own citizenry. In addition to the vast surveillance capabilities of the Golden Shield, Chinese authorities are also provided with advance passenger information (API) on those flying into and departing from China. This information contains a number of details related to the passenger, including the passenger's name, date of birth, gender, nationality, country of residence, travel document type, and passport information. The provision of this information to the authorities means that the government has detailed information on which passengers are aboard outbound flights. As such, the API provides another method by which the Chinese government is made aware of the coming and going of its citizens. The RPD found that, on a balance of probabilities, the Appellants' exit from China in October 2015, using their own passports, would have been reported to - and recorded by - Chinese authorities, and, as such, they would not need to enquire about the whereabouts of the Appellants as alleged.

The RPD further found that it was implausible in light of this objective evidence that the PSB would make multiple visits to the Appellants' home in China and essentially thwart its own efforts to apprehend the Appellants by providing them incentive not to return to China.

The Appellants submit the evidence in the record does not indicate that the PSB would necessarily have known that they had departed China. They argue that Response to Information Request CHN104762.E does not indicate that information sharing between Chinese government agencies has been fully realized. In addition, the Appellants submit that the documentary evidence indicates that the collection of API was for destination country. Finally, the Appellants submit that the multiple visits by the PSB to their family home is consistent with the documentary evidence which indicates that family members of Falun Gong practitioners can be harassed and punished by Chinese officials.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument. The RAD notes that the documentation states that security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens (also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield).4

An undated article on the website of the Ministry of Public Security, entitled: "Deepening the Implementation of the 'Golden Shield' Project" states that: ... all police units nationwide have access to eight public security databases, including the "National Basic Population Information Database" (China n.d.). Also accessible through the databases is information on household registration [hukou], border exit and entry, road traffic, and criminal investigations (ibid.).5

The RAD notes that the system has been used to track down Falun Gong practitioners. The Chinese economist writing in Open Magazine affirms that: ...Cisco's Policenet has been helping the [Chinese Communist Party]'s public security organs to ferret out political dissidents and Falun Gong practitioners for years (17 Feb. 2010).6

Furthermore, it is clear that airport officials have access to the PSB's databases. In 10 February 2014 correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Executive Director of the Dui Hua Foundation affirmed that airport security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities [also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield]. Similarly, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation stated that reports on "experiences of activists who have been detained while trying to board an international flight provide clear evidence that airport officials are connected to Policenet" (26 Feb. 2014). A colleague of Cao Shunli, who was also prevented from travelling to Geneva for the human rights training in September 2013, later publicized her own experience at the airport in Guangdong (HRIC 11 Oct. 2013). According to the Laogai research Foundation, the colleague indicates that when her passport was swiped by airport authorities, scanning equipment immediately made noises alerting airport officials that she was wanted by police. She was subsequently detained in the Guangdong Baiyun Airport and told that Shanghai police would not let her leave. She was then transported from Guangdong to Shanghai for detention and questioning. This woman's experience provides concrete evidence of airport officials coordinating with police departments in tracking and detaining a political dissident. (26 Feb. 2014)7

In addition, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation provided the following information: The Golden Shield incorporates extensive tracking and control mechanisms such as real-name online registration requirements, GPS monitoring, and facial recognition surveillance technology in a multi-pronged approach to identify potentially disruptive individuals. Policenet, a component of the Golden Shield, stores a wealth of information on Chinese citizens and connects the various agencies and levels of command within the public security apparatus. This integrated system enables Chinese public security forces to effectively target and neutralize political dissidents. (26 Feb. 2014)8

The RAD finds that the documentary evidence is clear that the system is integrated and that there is information sharing between Chinese government agencies. Accordingly, it is reasonable to expect that the PSB would have the tools available to them to track down the Appellants.

While it is true that RIR CHN105153 states that the "privacy policy" of the state-owned Air China airline indicates that the collection of API "is done solely for the immediate transmission to authorities of the destination country", the RAD finds that the preponderance of information in the same RIR states otherwise.

The RAD notes that the International Air Transport Association (IATA), an airline industry trade association that comprises 250 member airlines in 60 countries including China states that API can be provided inbound (to country of destination) or outbound (to country of departure), depending on states' preferences. In the case of China, the authorities want airlines to transmit API in both cases, i.e. when flying to and from China. (emphasis added)

Furthermore, the Malaysian National News Agency, Bernama, indicated in a March 2014 article that, according to "a travel industry source," regarding flight travel into China: China's Civil Aviation Administration has two control measures in place, the first being at the check-in counter at the foreign airport where a flight originates. The airline staff manning the counter needs to enter a passenger's passport details into the Advance Passenger Information System (APIS) where the particulars will be checked against China's Stop List. This is a list of people whom the Chinese authorities bar from boarding aircraft bound for any destination in the republic for reasons best known to the authorities there... [t]he second control measure is upon arrival in China, where the passports and the passengers again come under scrutiny before being allowed into the country.

In addition, RIR CHN104782.E states that Article 51 of the Exit and Entry Administration Law of the People's Republic of China requires that companies involved in the transportation of goods and passengers in and out of Chinese ports must declare information on the goods and passengers in advance of their departure or entry to the country.9 Accordingly, the RAD finds that objective evidence establishes that the PSB would have access to information on where the Appellants traveled and with which airline, and would be advised in advance of their return to China.

The RAD also agrees with the RPD and finds that given the alleged interest the PSB had in arresting the Appellants and given the PSB's ability to monitor the Appellants' departure from and return to China, it strains credulity that the PSB would expose their interest in the Appellants in the manner they are alleged.

The Appellants also submit that visits by PSB to family members of Falun Gong practitioners are consistent with the documentary evidence in the record. The RAD agrees with the Appellants that the objective evidence establishes that family members of practitioners can face serious consequences at the hands of the PSB. However, the RAD finds that the treatment of the Appellants family members is inconsistent with the objective evidence.

The RAD finds that country documentary evidence establishes that family members can face consequences solely because one member of their family is engaged in Falun Gong activities, regardless if they themselves were involved in Falun Gong activities. Although the Appellants have alleged that the PSB visited the home of the principal Appellant three times, there is no evidence that they suffered any significant consequences for the Appellants' failure to turn themselves into police. A 2008 report by the Falun Dafa Information Centre (FDIC), the official press office of the Falun Gong movement (FDIC n.d.), states that "[s]pouses, parents, children, and siblings of those who practice Falun Gong have suffered various degrees of persecution, ranging from loss of employment to torture" (FDIC 17 May 2008). In a telephone interview with the Research Directorate, a spokesperson for the Falun Dafa Association of Canada stated that some family members of practitioners have suffered the "same mistreatments as practitioners" themselves, including detention and torture (Falun Dafa 17 Sept. 2013). The 2008 report states that this allegedly includes pressuring spouses to divorce, threatening to end the careers of relatives, expelling the children of active Falun Gong members from school, and leaving some children orphaned or alone due to the detention or execution of one or both of their parents (FDIC 17 May 2008).10

In the context of this case, given the seriousness of the accusations, and where the PSB have arrested co-practitioners and are, according to the Appellants, continuing their pursuit of them, the RAD finds it is reasonable to expect that their family members would have experienced some greater sanctions in an effort to have the Appellants turn themselves into the PSB. However, the Appellants have not adduced any evidence to suggest that their family members have not been able to carry on their lives normally or that they have experienced any other sanctions.

The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that, given the alleged determination of the PSB to affect the arrest of the Appellants, it is reasonable to expect that the male Appellants' parents would have suffered some further sanctions to encourage the Appellants to return to Canada. The RAD finds that the lack of sanctions in light of the evidence undermines the allegations that the PSB are pursuing the Appellants in China. Lack of Police Issued Documents

The Appellants alleged that three of their fellow practitioners were arrested in China and that the PSB have attended their home on three occasions in pursuit of them; however, the PSB did not leave a summons or warrant for their arrest. Noting the documentary evidence in the record which states that the PSB issue summonses in criminal investigations, and that a summons may be left with an adult family member if the subject of interest is absent,11 the RPD drew an adverse credibility finding from the absence of any police documents which establish that the PSB are seeking them. The RPD found that, on a balance of probabilities, if the Appellants had been sought at home by the PSB on several occasions with the tenacity the Appellants have alleged, the PSB would have left a summons or a similar document at their home. The absence of these documents undermines the Appellants' allegations that they are being pursued by the PSB.

The Appellants submit that the RAD ought to not uphold this finding. They argue that the PSB engage in extrajudicial arrest and detention, and, as such, they would not necessarily leave a summons for the Appellants.

The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellants' argument in this regard. Though it is true that the documentary evidence cited by the Appellants indicates that there are cases where the PSB engage in extrajudicial arrest and detention, the RAD notes that the same evidence states that thousands of Falun Gong practitioners have been sentenced to prison indicating that practitioners were charged with offences relating to the practice of Falun Gong and tried in court. Still other evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for China12 indicates that, while many Falun Gong practitioners are held without due process, the authorities continue to criminally persecute and prosecute individuals and religious groups whom the authorities have declared "illegal" or "heretical".13

The current NDP states that Falun Gong practitioners in China are detained under Article 300 of China's Criminal Procedure Code, which deals with criminal involvement in evil cults.14 The NDP also indicates that the PSB issue summonses in criminal investigations, and that summons may be left with an adult family member if the subject of interest is absent.15

Minghui, a Falun Gong-affiliated website and volunteer organization dedicated to reporting on the Falun Gong community globally, with a focus on China, states that police arrested 1,187 Falun Gong practitioners in July 2015. Of those arrested, 126 practitioners were sent to brainwashing centres and 55 were sentenced to prison terms. Minghui further reports that between January and June 2015, 182 Falun Gong practitioners were arrested in Beijing; another 12 individuals were harassed in their homes but not arrested while 5 have been reported missing.16 Sources from 2014 and 2015 state that Falun Gong detainees are subjected to "brainwashing" or ideological "transformation" (China Aid 26 Aug. 2015; US 28 July 2014, 7; FDIC 9 Apr. 2015). According to the FDIC, this process is reported to involve sleep deprivation, threats, and being forced to watch videos vilifying Falun Gong (ibid.).17

According to the same document, the government of China launched a re-education campaign against the Falun Gong known as "the 2013-2015 final battle on education and transformation". The article also reports that the plan promotes "re-education centres" as the main venue for "transformation work" while "some documents also call for close cooperation with the judiciary to sentence practitioners to prison".18

After its own review of the documentary evidence, the RAD finds that, while authorities have been known to use extrajudicial methods to deal with Falun Gong practitioners, there is persuasive evidence that the government authorities use the police and judicial infrastructure to prosecute them. The RAD also accepts that there may be inconsistencies in this practice and that the PSB may not always leave warrants or summons with families. However, the RAD finds that the allegations of the Appellants suggest that the PSB are highly motivated to apprehend and goes beyond casual interest.

The RAD finds that, in light of the allegations made by the Appellants and given that the objective evidence suggests that police vigorously pursue Falun Gong practitioners, it is reasonable to expect that a summons or warrant would have been issued by the PSB to compel the Appellants to turn themselves in for investigation. The RAD agrees with the RPD and finds that the absence of any corroborating evidence from authorities that the PSB are pursuing the Appellants undermines their allegations in this regard.

On the basis of the totality of the adverse credibility findings made, the RAD agrees with the RPD and finds that the Appellants were not Falun Gong practitioners in China and that they are not being pursued by the PSB as alleged. The RAD notes that the Appellants do not challenge the RPD's findings with regard to their alleged practice of Falun Gong in Canada. In Summary

Having reviewed all of the evidence in this appeal, the RAD agrees with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants are not genuine Falun Gong practitioners in Canada and have never been genuine Falun Gong practitioners in China. The RAD further agrees with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants are not wanted by the authorities in China because of Falun Gong activities or for any other reason.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD and dismisses the appeal. (signed) "L. Favreau" L. Favreau September 14, 2016 Date 1 M.C.I. v.
